Free Kanji Apps: How to Choose Without Guesswork

Kanjidon Team · Jan 30, 2026

“Free kanji app” can mean fully free, ad-supported, a limited free tier or a trial that becomes a subscription. Listings and terms change, so a permanent ranking quickly becomes misleading. This guide gives you a repeatable way to inspect the current version of any app and decide whether it fits your study goal.

Define the Job Before Comparing Apps

Your immediate jobEvidence to look forA useful trial task
Recognize charactersClear prompts and contrast between similar formsTest several look-alike kanji in mixed order
Read vocabularyReadings taught inside words and examplesLearn a word, then read it in a new sentence
Review over timeA visible review queue and honest failure handlingFail an item and inspect what happens next
Practise handwritingStroke reference and input that matches your deviceWrite an unfamiliar item and compare with the model
Prepare for an examCoverage labels plus reading and listening practiceCheck claims against official JLPT samples

Check What “Free” Means Today

  • Read the current store listing and in-app purchase section in your region.
  • Identify which lessons, reviews or levels remain usable without payment.
  • Check whether a trial converts automatically and where it can be cancelled.
  • Look for ads, account requirements, data collection and internet dependence.
  • Treat screenshots and old reviews as historical evidence, not current terms.

Run the Same Learning Test in Every Candidate

  • Choose the same small set of unfamiliar words.
  • Complete the first learning session without changing defaults unnecessarily.
  • Return to the items through the app’s normal review path.
  • Check whether you can read the words outside the app, not only recognize its card layout.
  • Record friction: unclear prompts, excessive setup, inaccessible text or a queue you cannot control.

Inspect Privacy and Portability

Before investing a large study history, check what data the app collects, whether an account is required and what happens if you stop paying or change devices. If export or deletion matters to you, verify it in the current documentation rather than assuming every flashcard app supports it.

Avoid Building Three Competing Review Queues

A dictionary, reader and review app can complement one another because they do different jobs. Several spaced-review apps covering the same material often create duplicate work. Pick one primary queue, then use other tools for lookup, audio, writing or reading.

Make a Defensible Choice

  • The free access matches the task you actually need now.
  • Prompts test useful Japanese rather than app-specific recognition.
  • The review workload remains understandable and adjustable.
  • Current price and subscription terms are clear in your storefront.
  • Privacy, accessibility and account rules are acceptable to you.

Official Sources for Current Terms and Free Materials

  • Apple Support: view or cancel subscriptions
  • Google Play Help: manage subscriptions
  • Japan Foundation directory of Japanese learning materials
